Timeline::to_timeindex¶

Back to Timeline API Reference

Signature¶

TimeIndex Timeline::to_timeindex(bool require_sorted = true) const

Promote A Timeline Into An Ordered Index¶

to_timeindex() promotes a one-dimensional Timeline from general temporal storage into a TimeIndex: an object intended for ordered lookup, boundary searches, and time-based indexing. Promotion does not parse, sort, deduplicate, or change any instant. It validates that the existing values satisfy the stronger index contract and then returns a TimeIndex carrying those values and the same timezone.

Use this method when temporal values are about to become coordinates rather than ordinary data. Keep them as a Timeline when rank greater than one, NaT, or arbitrary ordering is meaningful. Promotion is therefore an explicit claim about structure, not a cosmetic type conversion.

Parameter¶

Parameter

Meaning

Default

require_sorted

Require nondecreasing epoch order during promotion

true

Setting require_sorted to false skips only the monotonicity check. It does not sort the values, and it does not relax the one-dimensional or no-NaT requirements. An unchecked, unsorted TimeIndex can be inspected or sorted, but ordered search operations do not have meaningful results until its order has been established.

Promotion Contract¶

Property

Required behavior

Rank

Exactly one; a scalar [] and matrix [m, n] are rejected

Length

Any nonnegative length, including an empty vector

Values

Every position must be a defined instant; NaT is rejected

Ordering

Nondecreasing by default; equal adjacent instants are allowed

Shape

The vector shape [n] is retained

Timezone

Retained exactly

Precision

Exact signed 64-bit epoch nanoseconds are retained

Nondecreasing order permits duplicates because ordering and uniqueness answer different questions. Call TimeIndex::is_unique when uniqueness is also required by the application.

Example: Sorted Duplicates Are Valid¶

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-01-03T00:00:00Z",
});
const auto index = times.to_timeindex();

std::cout << "size=" << index.size()
          << " increasing=" << std::boolalpha
          << index.is_monotonic_increasing()
          << " unique=" << index.is_unique() << '\n';

Output¶

size=3 increasing=true unique=false

The conversion preserves both copies of 1 January. It checks previous <= current, not previous < current.

Example: An Empty Axis Is A Valid Ordered Index¶

const auto index = pluss::timeline::epoch({0}).to_timeindex();

std::cout << "size=" << index.size()
          << " increasing=" << std::boolalpha
          << index.is_monotonic_increasing() << '\n';

Output¶

size=0 increasing=true

An empty vector has no pair that violates monotonic order. Notice that the factory receives shape {0}: a scalar has shape {} and cannot be promoted.

Example: Sortedness Is Checked By Default¶

const auto times = pluss::timeline::make({
    "2024-01-03T00:00:00Z",
    "2024-01-01T00:00:00Z",
});

try {
  (void)times.to_timeindex();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "rejected\n";
}

const auto unchecked = times.to_timeindex(false);
std::cout << "increasing=" << std::boolalpha
          << unchecked.is_monotonic_increasing() << '\n';

Output¶

rejected
increasing=false

The second call is not a sorting shortcut. It preserves [3 January, 1 January] exactly and records no promise that binary-search operations can repair that order. Prefer Timeline::sort() before promotion when an ordered index is the intended result.

Example: Strided Storage Is Materialized Safely¶

std::array<std::int64_t, 5> backing{
    1'704'067'200'000'000'000LL, 99,
    1'704'153'600'000'000'000LL, 88,
    1'704'240'000'000'000'000LL,
};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> shape{3};
const std::array<std::int64_t, 1> strides{2};

const auto times = pluss::Timeline::from_buffer(
    backing.data(), shape, strides, {}, "America/Edmonton");
const auto index = times.to_timeindex();

std::cout << pluss::timeline::print(index.timeline()) << '\n';

Output¶

Timeline(shape=[3], tz=America/Edmonton)
[ 2023-12-31 17:00:00, 2024-01-01 17:00:00, 2024-01-02 17:00:00 ]

The source reads every second entry of backing. Promotion copies those logical values into packed storage because index scans and binary searches require contiguous ticks. A contiguous receiver can share its reference-counted tick storage with the new index instead; in both cases, object lifetimes remain safe and the timezone is retained.

Example: Rank And NaT Remain Hard Invariants¶

const auto with_nat = pluss::timeline::make({"2024-01-01", ""});
const auto scalar = pluss::timeline::date("2024-01-01");
const auto matrix = pluss::timeline::date(
    std::vector<std::string>{"2024-01-01"}, {1, 1});

for (const auto* value : {&with_nat, &scalar, &matrix}) {
  try {
    (void)value->to_timeindex(false);
  } catch (const pluss::Error&) {
    std::cout << "rejected\n";
  }
}

Output¶

rejected
rejected
rejected

false cannot turn an absent instant into an index key or collapse an unsupported rank. Validation completes before a TimeIndex is returned.

Cost And Ownership¶

Promotion is linear in the number of elements because it validates every value and, by default, every adjacent ordering relation. A contiguous receiver shares its immutable, reference-counted tick storage with the result; a strided receiver incurs one linear materialization. The timezone string is retained by value. Neither path mutates the receiver.
